title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Myocardial infarction is a major cause of chest pain worldwide and is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Posterior myocardial infarction is a less common but clinically important subtype that is frequently underrecognized. Occlusion of the left circumflex artery or a dominant right coronary artery most commonly causes this condition, with established cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and hyperlipidemia contributing to its development. Disruption of blood flow produces ischemia and necrosis of the posterior left ventricular wall, often accompanied by inferior or inferolateral infarction. Isolated posterior myocardial infarction may present with vague symptoms or only subtle findings on examination.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Electrocardiographic features include horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3, prompting posterior lead placement to detect ST elevation. Prompt recognition and reperfusion therapy, including percutaneous coronary intervention or fibrinolysis, are critical to limit myocardial damage. Missed diagnosis increases the risk of complications such as cardiogenic shock, ventricular arrhythmias, and mechanical rupture. Early treatment improves survival and long-term outcomes.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance learners' competence in evaluating and managing posterior myocardial infarction. Participants will advance their mastery of the condition's etiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Improved skills will equip clinicians to collaborate with interprofessional teams providing care for affected individuals.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical and diagnostic features suggestive of posterior myocardial infarction, including electrocardiographic changes, cardiac biomarker abnormalities, and imaging findings. Implement evidence-based, individualized strategies for managing posterior myocardial infarction and mitigating its potential complications. Improve patient understanding of modifiable risk factors, medication adherence, and symptom recognition related to posterior myocardial infarction. Collaborate with the interprofessional team to educate, treat, and monitor patients experiencing posterior myocardial infarction to enhance functional and overall health outcomes. title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Introduction
content: Myocardial infarction is a major cause of chest pain and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Posterior wall myocardial infarction results from disruption of blood flow to the posterior myocardium, most often caused by occlusion of the left circumflex (LCx) artery or a dominant right coronary artery (RCA). The condition frequently co-occurs with inferior or inferolateral myocardial infarction. However, an isolated posterior wall myocardial infarction presents a significant diagnostic challenge.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Introduction
content: Diagnosis is often missed even when patients exhibit classic symptoms of myocardial infarction because electrocardiographic (ECG) findings can be subtle. A low threshold for additional evaluation with posterior leads should be maintained in patients with atypical or equivocal ECG changes, particularly ST depression in precordial leads V1 to V3. Prompt recognition is essential to guide reperfusion therapy and reduce the risk of adverse outcomes, including cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, and death. [1] Synthesized V7 to V9 leads may facilitate earlier diagnosis of isolated posterior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and improve prognosis. [2]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology
content: Obstruction or reduction of coronary blood flow causes myocardial infarction. The classic mechanism involves atherosclerotic plaque rupture or intraluminal thrombus formation, classified as type I myocardial infarction. Ischemia may also result from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand and supply, also known as type II myocardial infarction. Triggers include hypertension, hypotension, coronary artery spasm, anemia, sepsis, and arrhythmias.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology -- Coronary Anatomy
content: Posterior myocardial infarction results from disruption of the posterior coronary circulation. The coronary system consists primarily of the RCA and the left main coronary artery. The left main coronary artery is a short, wide-caliber vessel that bifurcates into the left anterior descending (LAD) artery and the LCx. In some individuals, a ramus intermedius branch arises from the angle between the left anterior descending and LCx.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology -- Coronary Anatomy
content: Approximately 70% of individuals have right-dominant circulation, in which the RCA gives rise to the posterior descending artery (PDA) and supplies the posterior myocardium. About 10% have left-dominant circulation, with the PDA originating from the LCx, while 20% have codominant circulation, where both the RCA and LCx contribute to the PDA. Occlusion of any of these vessels causes ischemia in the supplied territory, and the specific vessel responsible depends on the individual’s coronary anatomy (see Images . Isolated Posterior Myocardial Infarction, Graft Occlusion; Isolated Posterior Myocardial Infarction, Native Vessel Occlusion).

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology -- Risk Factors
content: Multiple risk factors predispose to coronary artery disease and, consequently, myocardial infarction. General risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity or metabolic syndrome, smoking, family history of premature coronary artery disease, sedentary lifestyle, male sex, and advanced age (older than 45 years in men and 55 years in women).

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology -- Risk Factors
content: The HEART (history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponin) score is a clinical decision tool used in patients older than 21 years who present with symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). This tool stratifies patients by risk and predicts the 6-week probability of a major adverse cardiac event.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Etiology -- Risk Factors
content: The HEART score is not used in patients with STEMI or other new ECG changes, hypotension, or comorbidities requiring admission, although the risk factors incorporated in this framework remain relevant for any patient in whom ACS is a concern. These risk factors include hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity (body mass index > 30 kg/m²), smoking (current or recent cessation within 3 months), relevant family history (parent or sibling with coronary vascular disease before age 65), and established atherosclerotic disease, including prior myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), coronary artery bypass grafting, cerebrovascular accident, transient ischemic attack, and peripheral arterial disease. [3]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Epidemiology
content: Posterior myocardial infarction accounts for approximately 15% to 21% of acute myocardial infarctions. The condition is frequently associated with inferior or lateral myocardial infarction, producing a large area of injury. The reported incidence of isolated posterior myocardial infarction is about 3.3% when posterior leads are employed, likely an underestimate given that posterior leads are not routinely obtained. [4]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Epidemiology
content: In a 2021 study, Shimojo et al retrospectively evaluated ST-segment changes on both standard 12-lead ECGs and synthesized V7 to V9 leads in patients with STEMI involving the LCx. STEMI was detected exclusively in the synthesized leads in 7% of patients (N=142). This subgroup demonstrated significantly higher rates of cardiac death at 3 months and 1 year (30.0% vs. 6.1%, P=0.031; 30.0% vs. 7.6%, P=0.050, respectively) and higher rates of mechanical complications (20.0% vs. 1.5%, P=0.025). These findings suggest that posterior myocardial infarction remains underrecognized, contributing to increased mortality.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Epidemiology
content: Several factors correlate with delayed presentation of ACS, including female sex, advanced age, Black or Hispanic race, lower educational attainment, and low socioeconomic status. Women are less likely to receive guideline-directed medical therapy or undergo cardiac catheterization. Men more often report central chest pain, whereas women frequently present with atypical symptoms, such as fatigue, dyspnea, indigestion, nausea or vomiting, palpitations, or generalized weakness. [5]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: Myocardial infarction results from a reduction or complete cessation of blood flow to myocardial tissue. Type 1 myocardial infarction, the most common subtype, occurs after rupture of a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque composed of macrophages, proliferating smooth muscle cells, and lipid-laden foam cells on an injured vascular wall. Complete or near-complete vascular occlusion causes little to no perfusion of the affected myocardium.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: Ischemia initiates metabolic and ionic disturbances within the myocardium. Prolonged ischemia leads to cardiomyocyte apoptosis, necrosis, and eventual cell death. Healing proceeds through scar formation, driven by an inflammatory cascade triggered by cytokines released from dying cells. Infiltrating phagocytes remove necrotic cells and extracellular matrix debris.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Pathophysiology
content: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system becomes activated, and transforming growth factor β promotes fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion with subsequent extracellular matrix deposition. These processes result in ventricular remodeling characterized by chamber dilation, scar formation, and progressive systolic dysfunction. Wall motion abnormalities are typically observed on echocardiography and may persist chronically. [6]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical
content: Chest pain is a frequent presenting complaint in the emergency department and warrants a broad differential diagnosis. The 6 life-threatening causes that must be rapidly excluded are acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical
content: Most patients presenting with acute chest pain undergo prompt ECG evaluation. Ischemic changes may be present, but management should not be guided by ECG findings alone. Comparison with prior ECGs is essential to determine chronicity. Failure to consider alternative diagnoses, such as aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism, risks delayed treatment and inappropriate interventions that may be life-threatening.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- History
content: A detailed history is essential, including onset, duration, provoking and relieving factors, pain quality, and associated symptoms. Posterior myocardial infarction typically presents with chest discomfort similar to other myocardial infarction types. Patients often describe a crushing substernal pressure rather than pain and may use expressions such as “an elephant sitting on my chest.” Radiation to the arms, jaw, or epigastrium is common. Symptoms may improve with nitroglycerin (NTG).

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- History
content: Although not definitive for distinguishing chest pain of cardiac origin from other etiologies, certain features can increase or decrease the likelihood of ACS. Chest discomfort associated with nausea or vomiting, diaphoresis, exertion, or strong emotion, as well as pain radiating to the arms or jaw, is more suggestive of ACS. Conversely, pain that is pleuritic, positional, sharp or stabbing, brief (< 1 minute), or reproducible on palpation lowers the probability of ACS but does not exclude the condition. When these latter characteristics are present, additional history is warranted to evaluate for alternative causes, including risk factors for pulmonary embolism such as unilateral leg swelling, recent surgery or trauma, prior pulmonary embolism or deep venous thrombosis, hormone use, recent immobilization, malignancy, or hemoptysis.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- History
content: Pain following an inciting injury or strain may indicate a musculoskeletal source. Abdominal causes such as gastroesophageal reflux, cholecystitis, or peptic ulcer disease should also be considered.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: The clinical presentation of myocardial infarction is variable. Patients may appear well or present in extremis. A focused physical examination should be performed in all patients with chest pain.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Vital signs should be obtained, including blood pressure measurements in both arms. Tachycardia is frequently observed, although bradycardia with or without atrioventricular block can occur when the RCA is involved, as it typically supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Arrhythmias may arise at any point during the course of myocardial infarction.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Blood pressure should be assessed carefully, as hypertension is common. However, hypotension can occur and is associated with increased mortality. The affected myocardium may be preload-dependent in isolated posterior infarction. Administration of NTG in this setting can precipitate profound hypotension. A marked discrepancy between blood pressures in each arm should prompt consideration of aortic dissection.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: The general appearance of the patient should be noted, including whether they are ill-appearing, diaphoretic, or in obvious distress. The presence of the Levine sign, in which the patient holds a clenched fist to the chest, should be recognized. Examination of the neck should include an assessment for jugular venous distention, which may indicate heart failure.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Cardiac examination should be performed with careful attention to murmurs and heart sounds. Acute mitral regurgitation caused by papillary muscle ischemia may be clinically silent or present with a new murmur. Regurgitant flow is best characterized by echocardiography with Doppler. Concomitant aortic stenosis should be considered, as the administration of NTG in such patients may result in significant hypotension. Distant heart sounds may suggest pericardial effusion and should raise concern for alternative etiologies, including aortic dissection with hemopericardium.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Pulmonary examination should include auscultation for bilateral rales, which may indicate heart failure. Asymmetric breath sounds should prompt evaluation for pneumothorax. Palpation of the chest wall should be performed to assess for tenderness, which may suggest a musculoskeletal source of pain. The presence of the Hamman sign or subcutaneous crepitus should be recognized as evidence of pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, or rib fracture.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Abdominal tenderness should prompt consideration of intra-abdominal pathology, such as cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may present with pain radiating to the chest or symptoms mimicking cardiac pain. Neurological assessment should be performed to identify any focal deficits, which may indicate aortic dissection with cerebral malperfusion.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Examination of the extremities should include evaluation for edema. Bilateral edema may indicate heart failure, whereas unilateral edema warrants investigation for deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Pulse deficits, mottling, or cool extremities suggest poor perfusion. Unilateral findings should again raise suspicion for aortic dissection.

content: Patients present in cardiac arrest in some cases. If the presenting rhythm is ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia, coronary angiography is recommended after return of spontaneous circulation has been achieved and the patient is hemodynamically stable for transfer.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation
content: A cardiac evaluation should be promptly initiated for patients presenting with chest pain suggestive of ACS, including a focused history and physical examination, ECG, and measurement of cardiac biomarkers. Rapid risk stratification enables the selection of appropriate medical therapy and urgent revascularization when indicated.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography
content: In a standard 12-lead ECG, a posterior myocardial infarction is observed indirectly due to anterior and lateral lead placement. Posterior myocardial infarction frequently occurs in association with inferior or lateral myocardial infarction. ST-segment elevation may be present if the infarction involves inferior, lateral, or inferolateral regions with posterior extension. Isolated posterior myocardial infarction does not produce ST-segment elevation on a typical ECG, and alternative ECG changes may be detectable. Placement of posterior leads (V7-V9) allows further evaluation of posterior involvement and requires positioning at specific anatomical landmarks, as follows: V7: Left posterior axillary line V8: Tip of the left scapula V9: Left paraspinal region [7] [8]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography
content: ST-segment elevation may be subtle in posterior myocardial infarction. Upward ST-segment displacement exceeding 0.5 mm in a single lead indicates posterior ischemia and is diagnostic for posterior STEMI. Comparison with previous ECGs is recommended whenever possible. Additional ECG changes that may be observed in posterior STEMI include the following: ST-segment depression in anterior leads, which may be deep (over 2 mm) and flat Large R wave in V2 to V3 (> 30 ms), exceeding the S-wave amplitude (R/S ratio greater than 1 in V2) Abnormal R-wave progression, defined as R waves in V2 to V3 larger than those in V4 to V6 Large, upright anterior T waves Signs of ischemia in inferior or lateral territories, including possible ST-segment elevation Mirror-image effect of posterior wall ischemia, in which tall anterior R waves become deep posterior Q waves, ST depression converts to ST elevation, and upright T waves invert. [9] [10]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography
content: Absence of these changes does not exclude posterior STEMI. [9] [10] The triad of horizontal or flat ST-segment depression, prominent positive QRS complexes in V1 or V2, and upright T waves demonstrates a positive predictive value for acute posterior myocardial infarction approaching 95%. [11]
contents: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Electrocardiography. Absence of these changes does not exclude posterior STEMI. [9] [10] The triad of horizontal or flat ST-segment depression, prominent positive QRS complexes in V1 or V2, and upright T waves demonstrates a positive predictive value for acute posterior myocardial infarction approaching 95%. [11]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Echocardiography
content: Posterior myocardial infarction is often clinically silent or may be missed on standard ECG views. Echocardiography provides complementary information to ECG and clinical assessment. A formal transthoracic echocardiogram should be obtained, but it must not delay revascularization in the setting of STEMI. Typical echocardiographic findings in posterior myocardial infarction include hypokinesia or akinesia of the inferolateral (posterior) wall and, when associated with inferior myocardial infarction, involvement of the inferior wall. Mitral regurgitation may be observed if the infarction affects mitral valve structures.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Investigation
content: Laboratory evaluation of posterior myocardial infarction is generally consistent with that for other types of myocardial infarction. Cardiac enzymes, particularly high-sensitivity troponin I or T, serve as the earliest and most specific markers, rising within 2 to 3 hours, peaking at 12 to 24 hours, and remaining elevated for 7 to 10 days. A complete blood count is obtained to exclude anemia or infection and evaluate platelet counts.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Investigation
content: Renal function, including blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and estimated glomerular filtration rate, should be assessed prior to contrast administration or initiation of medications. Serum electrolytes are measured to determine arrhythmia risk and ensure revascularization safety. Coagulation studies are also performed, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-proBNP may be considered when a large infarction is suspected. A metabolic profile, including hemoglobin A1C and lipid panel, is obtained to assess cardiovascular risk factors.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Reperfusion
content: The definitive management of acute posterior STEMI is reperfusion therapy. Once the diagnosis is established, the STEMI pathway should be activated. In patients presenting to a PCI-capable facility, primary PCI should be performed within 90 minutes of first medical contact (FMC). At non-PCI-capable facilities, fibrinolysis should be administered within 30 minutes if the anticipated delay to PCI exceeds 120 minutes. Routine early angiography or rescue PCI should be planned following fibrinolysis. The interval from FMC to device deployment constitutes a key quality metric for STEMI care, and all efforts should be made to minimize this interval, as myocardial salvage is time-dependent. [12]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Adjunctive Therapies
content: Adjunctive therapies in acute posterior STEMI include antiplatelet, anticoagulant, vasodilator, oxygen, and neurohormonal modulation strategies. Aspirin should be administered immediately upon suspicion of STEMI, either orally as a 325-mg chewable or rectally as a 600-mg suppository, as it reduces mortality. A P2Y12 inhibitor, such as prasugrel or ticagrelor, is recommended in preference to clopidogrel for patients undergoing PCI. Clopidogrel loading doses are 600 mg for STEMI and 300 mg for NSTEMI, each followed by 75 mg daily maintenance. Ticagrelor is administered as a 180-mg loading dose followed by 90 mg twice daily. Prasugrel is given as a 60-mg oral loading dose as early as possible, ideally prior to or at the time of PCI, followed by 10 mg orally once daily, typically continued for up to 12 months poststenting. [13]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Adjunctive Therapies
content: Anticoagulation is required to prevent thrombosis. Heparin should be administered after thrombolysis to reduce rethrombosis risk and during PCI to prevent procedural thrombosis. Alternative agents include low molecular weight heparin, fondaparinux, and bivalirudin.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Adjunctive Therapies
content: NTG should be administered sublingually for rapid absorption and onset of action. This agent promotes coronary vasodilatation and provides symptomatic relief of angina, although it does not reduce mortality. The most common adverse effect is headache, typically throbbing in nature. NTG should be avoided in inferior myocardial infarction due to the risk of hypotension, as the right ventricle is preload-dependent, and vasodilation reduces venous return. [14] Prior use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors, such as sildenafil, vardenafil, or tadalafil, within 24 hours must be assessed, as concurrent use with NTG can cause life-threatening hypotension. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors are used for erectile dysfunction and, in some cases, pulmonary hypertension.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Adjunctive Therapies
content: Oxygen therapy should be administered only if oxygen saturation is less than 90%. The AVOID (Air Versus Oxygen In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction) trial demonstrated that supplemental oxygen in nonhypoxic STEMI patients may increase early myocardial injury and is associated with larger infarct size at 6 months. [15] Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, including abciximab and eptifibatide, are no longer routinely used due to the advent of newer antiplatelet agents and stent technology, which reduce bleeding risk.

High-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, should begin as soon as possible.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Treatment / Management -- Postreperfusion Management
content: Patients should be monitored for complications, including mitral regurgitation, heart failure, and arrhythmias. Long-term management includes dual antiplatelet therapy for at least 12 months, high-intensity statin treatment, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker use (particularly in the presence of left ventricular dysfunction), β-blocker administration, lifestyle modification, and enrollment in cardiac rehabilitation programs.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Prognosis
content: Due to the more subtle ECG changes in isolated posterior myocardial infarction, the diagnosis is more likely to be delayed or missed compared with ischemia in other regions. When appropriately identified, no data demonstrate a significant difference in mortality between STEMI in the posterior wall and in other territories. Patients presenting with STEMI who undergo PCI within 2 hours exhibit 30-day mortality rates of 3% to 5%. Posterior extension of an inferior or lateral myocardial infarction produces more extensive myocardial injury, increasing the risk of adverse outcomes, including left ventricular dysfunction and death. [16] [17]

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Complications
content: Bradyarrhythmias Tachyarrhythmias Papillary muscle rupture, particularly of the posteromedial papillary muscle due to its single arterial supply (usually the RCA), which can result in acute severe mitral regurgitation Ventricular free wall rupture, less common in posterior myocardial infarction than in anterior myocardial infarction Ventricular septal rupture, if the infarction extends into the septum Right ventricular infarction, often associated with inferior or posterior myocardial infarction Left ventricular aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, with posterior pseudoaneurysms carrying a high risk of rupture [18] Heart failure and cardiogenic shock, secondary to acute mitral regurgitation Pericarditis Dressler syndrome

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Complications
content: Early reperfusion therapy and comprehensive postinfarction care are key to minimizing complications associated with this condition. Close surveillance for mechanical, electrical, and hemodynamic abnormalities allows timely intervention and improves outcomes.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Cardiovascular disease carries a high risk of morbidity and mortality. Patients should receive education regarding modifiable risk factors and strategies for their control. Established risk factors include tobacco use, diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia, while additional behavioral factors such as obesity, physical inactivity, and sedentary behavior independently contribute to risk. [19] Medications should be explained in detail, emphasizing adherence, as nonadherence to prescribed antiplatelet therapy can result in stent thrombosis. Consistent adherence to pharmacologic therapy combined with lifestyle modification reduces the likelihood of recurrent or progressive disease. Patients should also be counseled on recognizing symptoms suggestive of recurrent myocardial infarction and instructed to seek emergency care promptly.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Due to the significant morbidity and mortality associated with myocardial infarction, prevention and treatment require an interprofessional team. Prevention of cardiovascular disease in the outpatient setting is of critical importance and involves the patient’s primary care provider and other outpatient staff, including nurses, pharmacists, and dieticians. In the event of an acute myocardial infarction, first responders, typically emergency medical services, are responsible for transporting the patient to the emergency department, administering medications such as aspirin and NTG, and obtaining an initial ECG. If the ECG demonstrates STEMI, posterior or otherwise, the catheterization laboratory should be activated directly from the field. EMS may also provide resuscitation in patients with cardiac arrest secondary to STEMI.

title: Posterior Myocardial Infarction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: In the emergency department, physicians, advanced practice nurses, physician assistants, nursing staff, and technicians play a critical role in establishing the diagnosis of ACS, initiating resuscitation, and activating additional resources. An initial ECG should be performed within 10 minutes, and patients should undergo appropriate reperfusion therapy as soon as possible. Cardiologists are central to reperfusion therapy and ongoing stabilization and monitoring following myocardial infarction. In selected cases, a cardiothoracic surgeon may perform surgical management, such as coronary artery bypass grafting or valve replacement, depending on disease severity, comorbidities, and complications. Cardiology-specialized nursing supports these procedures, provides postoperative care, and communicates any changes in patient status to the cardiologist.

content: Patients initially require intensive care, with interprofessional staff monitoring for life-threatening complications and delivering appropriate interventions. After initial stabilization, ongoing care may involve dieticians, pharmacists, social workers, case managers, physical therapists, and occupational therapists to facilitate safe hospital discharge. Pharmacists review all medications upon arrival to the emergency department and throughout the postoperative and rehabilitative periods, verifying dosing, duration, and potential interactions, and informing the care team of any issues.
